plus-mode/0/p0.context: System note 'PLUS Mode: The Adaptive Rotor Speed Governor', section 'AVSR, and where PLUS mode sits inside it', paragraph
plus-mode/0/p0.text: AVSR — Adaptive Variable Speed Rotor — is the system that governs main rotor speed (NR). It does not hold NR at one fixed number; it varies the governing datum with airspeed (IAS), and that governing law itself varies linearly with density altitude between 8000 and 10000 ft (Figure 1-10, Operative NR envelope). Because the datum moves, the PFD markings move with it: a ±2% green band is shown around whatever the current datum is, with red indication and an aural warning at ±3% off datum.

autorotation-protection/1/p0.context: System note 'How Autorotation Protection Works', section 'Why torque is the trigger', paragraph
autorotation-protection/1/p0.text: In a steep, collective-mode-coupled descent, an AFCS chasing a vertical speed or approach path can keep reducing collective pitch to hold the demanded flight path. Torque below 15% means the engine is barely driving the rotor at all — pitch is being carried almost entirely by rotor inertia and airflow rather than engine power at that point. Reducing collective further from there is exactly the input that would tip the rotor system from powered flight into an actual autorotative state, without the pilot having deliberately chosen to enter one. The function puts a floor under how low the AFCS itself will command collective once torque is already that low, rather than let the automation walk the aircraft into autorotation on its own.
autorotation-protection/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

engine-and-fadec/4/p0.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section 'Starting', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/4/p0.text: The brushless starter-generator turns the engine for the start (see the Electrical Power System note). A CRANK switch per engine drives a dry motoring cycle. Duty-cycle limits: after the first start attempt wait 30 seconds, after the second another 30 seconds, after the third wait 30 minutes. Motoring is one of 45 s on / 10 min off, 30 s on / 5 min off, or 15 s on / 2 min off — repeatable three times, then a 30-minute rest.
engine-and-fadec/4/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

engine-and-fadec/6/p1.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section '1(2) ENG FAIL FIXED', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/6/p1.text: The problem is a torque split: with one engine's power frozen and the other following the rotor, the two torques diverge. A split over 30% brings up the 1(2) ENG DEGR caution on the higher-torque engine. Below that, monitor and land as soon as practicable. During descent, do not let the good engine's torque fall below 10%.
engine-and-fadec/6/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

engine-and-fadec/6/p2.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section '1(2) ENG FAIL FIXED', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/6/p2.text: How the affected engine is handled depends on where its torque froze. At or below 50%, it can be left running: consider the low power available on that engine during landing, and after touchdown lower the collective smoothly to MPOG while keeping NR within limits. If NR rises above the limit, shut down the affected engine before lowering the collective to MPOG. Above 50%, before the approach, the RFM refers to the SINGLE ENGINE PROCEDURE. If the affected engine is above MCP, consider shutting it down within 30 minutes to avoid exceeding limitations, and expect possible NR droop and a large torque variation on the other engine when it is shut down.
engine-and-fadec/6/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/0/p1.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p1.text: Generation is two brushless starter-generators, one per engine. During start they run as motors, turning the engine; once the engine is running they generate. Each is managed by its own Brushless Control Unit (BCU) in the rear fuselage under the cargo compartment — the BCU does the AC-to-28VDC conversion in generation mode and the reverse in start mode.
electrical-system/0/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p0.text: The Electrical Power Generation and Distribution System (EPGDS) generates AC power, converts it to 28 VDC, and distributes it. There is no usable AC bus — AC exists only internally between the generators and their control units; every load on the aircraft is 28 VDC.
electrical-system/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/0/p2.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p2.text: Two Nickel-Cadmium batteries in the rear avionic bay: a 33 Ah main battery (MAIN BATT) and a 13 Ah auxiliary battery (AUX BATT). Optional kits substitute higher-capacity units (44 Ah main; 28 Ah or 33 Ah auxiliary). The batteries start the engines when no ground power is connected, and are the sole power source after a double generator failure. On the ground the system can instead be fed by a DC Ground Power Unit — recommended for engine starts after a cold soak.
electrical-system/0/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/0/p3.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p3.text: Distribution is solid-state (SSEPM): instead of a wall of mechanical circuit breakers and relays, power is routed through Remote Electrical Power Units (REPUs) — two in the nose compartment, one in the rear fuselage — fed from two DC Power Distribution Units (DC PDU 1 and DC PDU 2) in the rear avionic bay. The DC PDUs do the contactor switching, bus voltage and current monitoring, and over/under-voltage and overcurrent protection. A conventional Circuit Breaker Panel on the overhead console still feeds the emergency buses directly.
electrical-system/0/p3.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/5/p1.text: 1(2) DC GEN HOT (overheat) — switch the affected generator off immediately. Same result: one generator carries the aircraft, all non-essential buses lost.
electrical-system/5/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/6/p1.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing both generators — ELEC FAIL', paragraph
electrical-system/6/p1.text: Battery power lasts a maximum of 30 minutes — that is the number that drives everything else. Land as soon as possible.
electrical-system/6/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/7/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Related failures', paragraph
electrical-system/7/p0.text: 1(2) EMER BUS FAIL — a single emergency bus is lost while generation is otherwise normal. The losses are specific and worth knowing: EMER BUS 1 takes VHF 1, the standby instrument (ESIS), engine 1 fire detection and extinguisher, and AFCS force-trim release; EMER BUS 2 takes the pilot's EDCU, PFD, master warning/caution lights, landing light, RAD ALT 2, engine 2 fire detection and extinguisher, NAV 2, GPS 2, and the transponder. Reduce speed and continue attentive.
electrical-system/7/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

fire-protection/0/p2.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'What it is', paragraph
fire-protection/0/p2.text: Engine extinguishing is two identical, interchangeable stainless-steel bottles charged with HALON 1301 and nitrogen, mounted between the engine ejectors under the rear fairing. They are cross-connected: either bottle can be fired into either engine bay. Each bottle has a temperature-compensated pressure sensor that drives a low-pressure caption.
fire-protection/0/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/6/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing both generators — ELEC FAIL', paragraph
electrical-system/6/p0.text: A double DC generator failure triggers the "WARNING WARNING" aural and the ELEC FAIL warning. First actions: pilot utility light ON (for night operations), then GEN 1 & 2 to RESET and confirm ON. If ELEC FAIL remains, the aircraft is on battery power: all main buses and all non-essential buses are lost, and only the emergency and essential buses remain. The RFM warns that battery power is available for a maximum of 30 minutes.
electrical-system/6/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/5/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing one generator', paragraph
electrical-system/5/p0.text: 1(2) DC GEN FAIL — reset the affected generator (RESET, then confirm ON); if it stays failed, switch it off and let the other one carry the load. With BUS TIE CLOSED the remaining generator supplies power and only the non-essential buses are lost; if BUS TIE stays OPEN (try BUS TIE RESET on the EDCU ELEC page first), the affected generator's main buses (1 and 3, or 2 and 4) are lost as well as all non-essential buses. Non-essential buses can be brought back selectively with the NON ESS L/R OVRD switches. Watch the surviving generator's load on the MFD and reduce electrical load if the limit is exceeded.
electrical-system/5/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

fire-protection/1/p0.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'What an engine fire looks like', paragraph
fire-protection/1/p0.text: An ENG 1(2) FIRE gives, together: the CAS warning message, the "ENG 1(2) FIRE" audio tone with the master warning flashing, a red FIRE light on the fire control panel, a red warning light on that engine's control panel, and the engine silhouette turning red on the MFD PWR PLANT format.
fire-protection/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

fire-protection/2/p0.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'The two controls', paragraph
fire-protection/2/p0.text: ENG 1(2) FIRE/ARM push-button (guarded) — pressing it shuts that engine down by closing its fuel shut-off valve, and also closes the heating-system bleed shut-off valve. It arms the extinguishing circuit for that bay.
fire-protection/2/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

fire-protection/3/p2.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'Engine bay fire in flight', paragraph
fire-protection/3/p2.text: If the warning does not clear, fire BTL 2. If it still does not clear after the second bottle: LAND IMMEDIATELY and carry out the EMERGENCY GROUND EGRESS procedure — there is nothing left to fight it with.
fire-protection/3/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

fire-protection/3/p0.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'Engine bay fire in flight', paragraph
fire-protection/3/p0.text: Confirm the fire light on the engine control panel, establish a safe OEI flight condition, then take the affected ENG MODE knob to IDLE, confirm the fire, and take it to OFF. Lift the guard and press that engine's FIRE ARM push-button, then set FIRE EXTING to BTL 1 and wait for the 1 FIRE BTL LOW P caption.
fire-protection/3/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

electrical-system/6/p2.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing both generators — ELEC FAIL', paragraph
electrical-system/6/p2.text: If a load on MAIN BUS 1 is genuinely required, GEN BUS to OVRD feeds it from the battery — and BUS TIE to OVRD additionally feeds MAIN BUS 2 — but each override shortens the 30 minutes. The landing gear control is on a bus that is lost in flight in this state, so the gear has to be put down with the LANDING GEAR EMERGENCY DOWN procedure; VHF 1 is selected on the right side to keep radio contact. A subsequent MAIN BATT OFF caution means land as soon as possible, without qualification.
electrical-system/6/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

weather-radar/0/p0.context: System note 'Weather Radar RTA-4112', section 'What it is', paragraph
weather-radar/0/p0.text: A fully automatic radar that displays significant weather data at all available ranges and altitudes, at all times, with a clutter-free display. It also does beacon detection and terrain mapping. Hardware: a 12 in flat-plate antenna in the nose radome, an antenna drive unit (moves the antenna up to 120° in azimuth, 32° in elevation), and a transceiver with separate receivers for weather and beacon signals, feeding the PFDs and MFD.
weather-radar/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

About a 10-second discharge, effective on small carbonaceous, flammable-liquid, and electrical fires. Any extinguisher that has been used must be replaced at the first opportunity, even if it still has agent in it.

weather-radar-rdr-1600/0/p1.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', section 'What it is', paragraph
weather-radar-rdr-1600/0/p1.text: It provides three families of modes: air-to-surface search and detection (SR1/SR2/SR3), weather avoidance (WX/WXA), and beacon detection/navigation (BCN).

weather-radar-rdr-1600/0/p0.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', section 'What it is', paragraph
weather-radar-rdr-1600/0/p0.text: The Telephonics RDR-1600 is a multi-mode surveillance and weather radar built for maritime missions. Hardware: a 12 in flat-plate antenna and drive unit, a receiver/transmitter unit, an interface unit, and a static inverter. ADAHRS 1/2 data are used for antenna stabilization. Controlled through the MFD drop-down menu and the CCD, displayed on the PFDs and/or MFD.

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r0.text: Mode: SR1 (Search 1); What it does: Sea clutter rejection — short transmitted pulse with clutter-rejection circuitry, for short-range mapping of targets in a sea-clutter environment. Detects surface targets down to 500 ft minimum range.; Notes: Active only at 10 NM range or below; at 20 NM or greater the transmitter switches to a long pulse and clutter rejection disengages (behaves like SR3)
weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r1.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', table 'Operating modes', one row (columns ['Mode', 'What it does', 'Notes'])
weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r1.text: Mode: SR2 (Search 2); What it does: Short-range precision ground mapping — short transmitted pulse. Detects surface targets down to 500 ft minimum range.; Notes: Active only at 10 NM range or below; at 20 NM or greater it effectively becomes SR3
weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r2.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', table 'Operating modes', one row (columns ['Mode', 'What it does', 'Notes'])

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r4.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', table 'Operating modes', one row (columns ['Mode', 'What it does', 'Notes'])
weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r4.text: Mode: WXA (Weather Alert); What it does: As WX, but red storm-cell areas flash, and the Target Alert function activates: it warns the pilot if a red storm cell is detected within 25 NM beyond the selected range and within ±10° of boresight — including when the pilot isn't looking at the weather display.; Notes: Alert range 25 NM beyond selected range, ±10° boresight

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r3.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r5.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', table 'Operating modes', one row (columns ['Mode', 'What it does', 'Notes'])
weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/r5.text: Mode: BCN (Beacon); What it does: Interrogates and receives pulses from a fixed transponder on a dedicated beacon frequency. Selectable Mode A (0–9) or DO-172 Mode B (0–15) code.; Notes: Up to 160 NM, depending on beacon sensitivity/power

weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/note.context: System note 'Weather Radar RDR-1600', section 'Operating modes', table note
weather-radar-rdr-1600/1/note.text: Weather and search modes cannot run at the same time, but any of them can be paired with Beacon: WX/BCN, WXA/BCN, SR1/BCN, SR2/BCN, or SR3/BCN. htaws/0/p0.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'What it does', paragraph
htaws/0/p0.text: HTAWS, embedded in the Collins MFD-2810, gives terrain and obstacle awareness through two independent functions: Forward Looking Terrain (and Obstacle) Alerting (FLTA), which looks ahead of the aircraft's flight path, and Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS), which reacts to the aircraft's actual proximity to terrain. Terrain/obstacle display is selectable on PFD and MFD; an obstacle is defined as any human-made structure higher than 50 ft AGL.

htaws/3/p1.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'SAR mode and the offshore approach exception', paragraph
htaws/3/p1.text: On an offshore approach with OFFSHORE mode selected, SINK RATE / PULL UP alerts (GPWS Mode 1 OFSH caution/warning) can be generated at glide path angles greater than 3°.
htaws/3/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

htaws/3/p0.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'SAR mode and the offshore approach exception', paragraph
htaws/3/p0.text: SAR mode reduces the FLTA height threshold down to as low as 30 ft AGL, for genuinely low-height flight. Like the other reduced-sensitivity modes (LOW ALT, TACT ALT, OFF AIRPORT), SAR must not be selected under IMC — except when performing an offshore-platform IFR approach or other special IFR procedure, which is exactly the case this EP option exists to support.
htaws/3/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

htaws/5/p0.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'Inhibiting and status messages', paragraph
htaws/5/p0.text: TAWS INHIBIT disables all alerts except altitude callouts (the terrain map image stays up). AUDIO INHIB mutes cautions only — not callouts, not warnings — and clears itself after 5 minutes if not deselected first. OFF APT reduces nuisance alerts when landing somewhere not in the database, without disabling the system. G/S CANCEL suppresses the glideslope-deviation alert when the ILS isn't in the database — it has no effect when OFFSHORE mode is selected.
htaws/5/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

htaws/5/p1.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'Inhibiting and status messages', paragraph
htaws/5/p1.text: Failure captions: TAWS FAIL (no valid HTAWS info — both FLTA and GPWS gone), TERRAIN (terrain data unavailable), GPWS INOP, FLTA INOP, OBST INOP (obstacle database missing, or too many obstacles in view — the system only ever displays the 100 nearest above the altitude clearance level).
htaws/5/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

svs/0/p0.context: System note 'Synthetic Vision System (SVS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
svs/0/p0.text: SVS, embedded in the Collins MFD-2810, builds a three-dimensional synthetic view of the terrain around the aircraft from precise navigation sensor inputs plus a high-resolution terrain, obstacle and runway/heliport database. It displays airport runways and helipads, obstacles higher than 50 ft, and a Flight Path Vector (FPV) showing the aircraft's actual trajectory. Selected on the PFD's attitude/navigation area via the PFD menu or the on-side DCP; the FPV and obstacle layers can be switched off independently.
svs/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

digital-map/0/p0.context: System note 'Digital Map System', section 'What it is', paragraph
digital-map/0/p0.text: A moving-map display selectable to underlay the FPLN page on the MFD (DMAP item on the MFD menu). The system can receive two DMAP video sources, DMAP1 and DMAP2, either selectable from the DMAP menu. Like the weather radar and HTAWS, it must not be used for navigation — it is an awareness tool, and the display/database may not have the accuracy to base routine navigation decisions or route planning on.

svs/2/p0.context: System note 'Synthetic Vision System (SVS)', section 'When it turns off on its own', paragraph
svs/2/p0.text: SVS must not be used for navigation, and must not be selected ON during approach and landing. It won't display at all with the central MFD powered off or reverted to PFD format. It is automatically inhibited whenever aircraft attitude exceeds 30° nose up/down or 50° bank left/right, and re-selects itself automatically once attitude comes back within ±10° pitch and ±5° roll.

opls/0/p0.context: System note 'OPLS: Obstacle Proximity LiDAR System', section 'What it is', paragraph
opls/0/p0.text: OPLS gives visual and audio obstacle-distance awareness while hovering or in low-speed flight. Three LiDAR (Laser Imaging Detection and Ranging) units are mounted around the transmission cowling below the rotor head; their three overlapping beams are digitally mixed to produce 360° obstacle coverage — but only in the plane of the sensor units. Nothing above or below that plane is detected.
opls/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

htaws/2/note.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'Alerts', table note
htaws/2/note.text: Aural-only messages with no caption: THREE HUNDRED (priority 4) and, when enabled, the active height callouts (200/100/50/40/30/20/10 ft). Cautionary alerts annunciate once; warning alerts repeat until the condition clears. TOO LOW TERRAIN and CHECK AIRSPEED are generated when OFFSHORE mode has been selected. SINKRATE is the amber alert for an excessive descent rate compared with height above terrain when the FLTA function is not available or the helicopter's groundspeed is below 40 kt.
htaws/2/note.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

opls/0/p1.context: System note 'OPLS: Obstacle Proximity LiDAR System', section 'What it is', paragraph
opls/0/p1.text: Controlled from a dedicated OPLS page on the EDCU (Home → KITS → MIS tab → OPLS tab): POWER, MAINT, MUTE, INFO buttons, plus a status indicator. Displayed on the MFD as a plan-view polar grid of the obstacle profile around the helicopter, selected via the cursor control device (VIDEO → OPLS) or the MFD's T4 top bezel key.
opls/0/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

evs-camera/0/p1.context: System note 'EVS Camera', section 'What it is', paragraph
evs-camera/0/p1.text: The camera automatically recalibrates its IR sensor (NUC) every 4 minutes — a 1-second screen blank with CAL displayed — which can be inhibited from the same EDCU page if needed. It's self-anti-iced with internal heaters whenever powered on, fed from Main Bus 1 (REPU 1 Channel A), a bus not shown on the DC ELEC synoptic page.
evs-camera/0/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

evs-camera/1/p0.context: System note 'EVS Camera', section 'Display and field of view', paragraph
evs-camera/1/p0.text: Shown full-size on the MFD VIDEO page, or as picture-in-picture on VIDEO or DMAP pages. Brightness/contrast adjust via the VIDEO page bezel buttons — on the EVS-2300, the IR and color channels have independent brightness/contrast controls. Field of view (Narrow/Wide) is selected from the PFD EVS menu or the DCP EVS button, and on the EVS-2300 that selection applies to both the IR and color image together. Zooming is available via PFD controls or the DCP.
evs-camera/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

ehps/0/p0.context: System note 'EHPS: Electric Motor-Driven Hydraulic Power Supply', section 'What it is', paragraph
ehps/0/p0.text: A 28 VDC electric motor-driven hydraulic pump installed on hydraulic system 1, ground use only. It provides just enough hydraulic pressure to do the full-and-free flight-controls check on the servo-actuators before either engine — and its mechanically-driven hydraulic power supply — is even running. Controlled from the EDCU HYD page, powered from the helicopter battery, and limited by AMMC logic to 2 minutes of operation maximum. In flight, switching it on is inhibited by design.
ehps/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

ehps/1/p0.context: System note 'EHPS: Electric Motor-Driven Hydraulic Power Supply', section 'Why it changes the start sequence', paragraph
ehps/1/p0.text: Without EHPS, engine 1 normally has to start in ACC (accessory) mode first, because the flight-controls check needs mechanically-driven hydraulic pressure that only comes from a running engine. EHPS removes that dependency: run the electric pump on the ground, do the flight-controls check off it, then engine 1 can be started directly in MAIN mode, either engine first. The equivalent flight-controls check step later in the normal Engines Start procedure is skipped, since it's already been done.
ehps/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

evs-camera/0/p0.context: System note 'EVS Camera', section 'What it is', paragraph
evs-camera/0/p0.text: Two possible installations: the MAX-VIZ EVS-1500, IR image only, or the EVS-2300, which adds a color image alongside the IR one. A Long Wave Infrared camera is mounted facing forward under the right-hand nose compartment, feeding the MFD as a visual aid in reduced visibility. Selected on and off from the EDCU KITS → CAMERA tab; a video test pattern shows for about 5 seconds after power-on, then an OK message, then an IR image after about 20 seconds total.
evs-camera/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/1/p0.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'What is on the display', paragraph
esis/1/p0.text: The attitude display has a pitch ladder marked every 2.5° within ±7.5° of the horizon and every 5° out to ±90°, a roll scale with pointer, and a slip trapezoid under the pointer that stops at ±10° of slip. The airspeed tape shows an 80 kt window, with a line every 10 kt and figures every 20 kt. Below 20 kt the digital readout shows 0 in black on amber. At or above VNE the digits turn white on red. A solid red bar marks VNE with both engines operating, and a dashed red and white bar marks VNE one engine inoperative.
esis/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/1/p1.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'What is on the display', paragraph
esis/1/p1.text: The altitude readout runs from −2,000 ft to 40,000 ft, vertical speed reads to ±9,950 ft/min in 50 ft/min steps, and metric altitude can be selected on installations that support it. A magnetic heading tape shows ±30° around the current heading. When a NAV source is selected the ESIS also draws a VOR or ILS display with course, deviation, localizer and glideslope scales and inner, middle and outer marker indications.
esis/1/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/3/p0.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Power', paragraph
esis/3/p0.text: The ESIS is fed from EMER BUS 1. It is listed among the services lost with a 1 EMER BUS FAIL, together with the pilot clock (where no digital clock is fitted), VHF 1, engine 1 fire detection and extinguisher, and the AFCS force trim release, so that failure takes the standby instrument away at the same time as it degrades the rest of the cockpit.
esis/3/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/3/p1.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Power', paragraph
esis/3/p1.text: Where the optional ADI STBY Emergency Battery is installed, it keeps the standby attitude indicator alive for at least 30 minutes after a total loss of generation. That is a separate note in this section. On the ground it is checked in the engine pre-start checks: hold ADI STBY BATT TEST until TEST illuminates, release, then set ARM.
esis/3/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/4/p1.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Where the RFM tells you to use it', paragraph
esis/4/p1.text: AHRS miscompare (roll or pitch differing by ±5°, vertical speed by ±200 ft/min): compare with the ESIS to establish which AHRS is giving correct data, then switch to it on the RCP. After an AHRS FAIL and the reconfiguration to the good AHRS, both attitude indicators use the same source, so the procedure ends with monitoring PFD attitude against the ESIS.
esis/4/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

ehps/2/p0.context: System note 'EHPS: Electric Motor-Driven Hydraulic Power Supply', section 'The check itself', paragraph
ehps/2/p0.text: ELEC PUMP switch on, confirm HYD 1 pressure reads 80–120 bar (this is genuinely in the pump's normal red zone on the gauge — don't read that as a fault). Exercise the controls progressively and slowly: collective to about 50% then cyclic to full displacement, cyclic centered then collective to full displacement, then pedals to full displacement. Deselect ELEC PUMP when done — it also disengages on its own after 2 minutes regardless.
ehps/2/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/4/p2.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Where the RFM tells you to use it', paragraph
esis/4/p2.text: ADS failure: after moving the ADS knob on the RCP to the good system, both air data indicators use the same source, and the procedure again ends with monitoring PFD airspeed and altitude against the ESIS. Vertical speed is not recovered by ADS reconfiguration. If vertical speed is needed, reduce speed to no more than 120 KIAS, continue attentive and disengage the AP channel associated with the failed ADS side.
esis/4/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/5/p1.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'AP DEGR: the autopilot watches it too', paragraph
esis/5/p1.text: Both cases then share the same actions: reduce speed to no more than 120 KIAS, continue attentive, and use only the permitted AFCS upper modes, which are HOV, TDH and TU, plus the coupled approach modes VAPP, LOC/GS, NAPP and NLOC/NGS.
esis/5/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/6/p0.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Numbers and corrections', paragraph
esis/6/p0.text: The ESIS has its own airspeed calibration curve in Section 4 (Figure 4-6, ESIS indicator), separate from the one for the primary displays. Indicated altitude on the cockpit instruments is within ±30 ft (9 m) throughout the speed range.
esis/6/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/6/p1.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Numbers and corrections', paragraph
esis/6/p1.text: With the ALTERNATE static source selected (STATIC source switch, guard removed, with ECS set to BACKUP), the source is cabin air and the altimeter reading must be decreased by 200 ft (60 m). Selecting it may also cause AVSR FAIL, with NR fixed at 103%. The pitot-static probes supply pressure to the air data unit and to the standby instrument.
esis/6/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

adi-stby-battery/0/p0.context: System note 'ADI STBY Emergency Battery', section 'What it is', paragraph
adi-stby-battery/0/p0.text: A dedicated Li-Ion battery, installed in the left side of the nose avionics bay, that automatically feeds the standby attitude indicator for at least 30 minutes after a total failure of the electrical generating system. It connects through the CB panel to EMER BUS 1, protected by a 7.5A ADI STBY circuit breaker — a self-contained backup for exactly one instrument, not the wider emergency bus.
adi-stby-battery/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

esis/2/p0.context: System note 'ESIS: The Standby Instrument', section 'Controls', paragraph
esis/2/p0.text: Three controls on the bezel: the M (menu) button, the SET knob and the ALN button. Pressing M steps through brightness (BRT), NAV1/NAV2 source, course (CRS), pressure unit (HPA/IN) and altitude unit (feet or metres), and the SET knob scrolls and sets the chosen item. ALN is the attitude align button. NAV1 and NAV2 information is always displayed in green.
esis/2/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

adi-stby-battery/0/p1.context: System note 'ADI STBY Emergency Battery', section 'What it is', paragraph
adi-stby-battery/0/p1.text: Controlled by a Control Switch Annunciator on the right side of the interseat console, three positions: ARM (battery powered through EMER BUS 1, ready to supply output), OFF (disconnected from both EMER BUS 1 and the ADI STBY), and TEST (press and hold — checks state of charge is above 80% plus the internal heater and temperature monitoring; TEST illuminates green if it passes). The STBY annunciator itself lights amber whenever the battery is actually delivering power to the ADI.
adi-stby-battery/0/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

automatic-search-modes/0/p2.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'What the mode chain is for', paragraph
automatic-search-modes/0/p2.text: One important, separate limitation this option unlocks: IMC flight below Vmini (50 KIAS) is only permitted when Automatic Search Modes are in use — not otherwise.
automatic-search-modes/0/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

automatic-search-modes/1/p0.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'HOV, MOT, and WTR in a little more detail', paragraph
automatic-search-modes/1/p0.text: HOV is the underlying basic AFCS mode this all builds on — no dedicated option file required — using AHRS ground velocity to hold hover position or low-speed flight, transitioning automatically from velocity-hold to position-hold once groundspeed falls below 1.5 kt. RHT engages automatically under it if a valid radar altimeter signal is available; ALT substitutes if not.
automatic-search-modes/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

automatic-search-modes/1/p1.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'HOV, MOT, and WTR in a little more detail', paragraph
automatic-search-modes/1/p1.text: MOT engages via its own AFCS Control Panel button, available with groundspeed at or below 150 kt and selected radar height between 150 and 2000 ft AGL. It offsets the resulting hover position downwind and to the left of the marked point, adjustable in the range 0–150 ft on the EDCU.
automatic-search-modes/1/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

automatic-search-modes/1/p2.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'HOV, MOT, and WTR in a little more detail', paragraph
automatic-search-modes/1/p2.text: WTR only exists with the Rescue Hoist kit installed (Supplement 5). Once selected, the hoist operator can adjust the aircraft's hover groundspeed up to ±10 kt from the pilot's HOV reference, using the hoist pendant's five-position switch — pilot input always overrides the hoist operator's input.
automatic-search-modes/1/p2.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

automatic-search-modes/2/r1.text: Mode: WTR; Engagement range: HOV mode engaged; MUH: 30 ft AGL

automatic-search-modes/2/r2.text: Mode: NGSPD (FMS groundspeed control); Engagement range: 50–180 kt groundspeed, 50 KIAS to Vne; MUH: 150 ft AGL

automatic-search-modes/2/note.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'Engagement and minimum use height', table note
automatic-search-modes/2/note.text: TDH, TU and MOT may only engage over flat surfaces clear of obstructions. Over the sea, MUH must be increased relative to the maximum reported/observed wave height. NGSPD carries the same Airspeed Envelope Protection logic as GSPD elsewhere in the AFCS — it intervenes if the groundspeed datum would push airspeed below Vmini or above Vne − 5.

automatic-search-modes/3/p0.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'Collective Safety Function, search-mode-specific thresholds', paragraph
automatic-search-modes/3/p0.text: With search modes engaged, the low-height floor is 18 ft AGL when MOT, TU or TDH is active in hover/low-speed condition, or 90 ft AGL when MOT or TD is active in cruise condition — hover/low speed being below 55 KIAS or HOV/TDH engaged, cruise being above 55 KIAS with neither engaged. As elsewhere in the AFCS, breaching one of these inadvertently causes the system to add collective automatically back to the threshold.

automatic-search-modes/0/p0.context: System note 'Automatic Search Modes', section 'What the mode chain is for', paragraph
automatic-search-modes/0/p0.text: Applicable to Avionic Phase 8.0 and later (Supplement 54). Together, these AFCS modes fly an automated profile from cruise down to a stabilized hover over a target, and back up again — the profile a SAR or offshore search actually flies, without the pilot hand-flying every axis through the transition.

external-hoist/0/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'What it is', paragraph
external-hoist/0/p0.text: A Goodrich hoist unit mounted on the right side of the cabin, in either a 290 ft or 165 ft usable-cable version, each with its own pendant. The pilot and copilot can operate the hoist from the collective grip; the Hoist Operator (HO) operates it from the control pendant, which also displays cable payout. Pilot control always overrides the HO's input. Maximum load: 249 kg (550 lb) above 0°C OAT, 227 kg (500 lb) at or below — maximum 2 persons plus equipment either way.
external-hoist/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

external-hoist/1/p1.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Key limitations', paragraph
external-hoist/1/p1.text: During hoist operations the pilot must either fly manually, or fly attentively if HOV and RHT (or ALT) modes are engaged — the autopilot is not a substitute for monitoring during a hoist operation. Maximum weight including the hoisted load is 4800 kg (above 4600 kg for takeoff/landing, the Supplement 30 increased-gross-weight configuration is required). The HO must be harnessed throughout, wear protective gloves, and guide the cable by hand.
external-hoist/1/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

external-hoist/2/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Cable and hoist malfunctions', paragraph
external-hoist/2/p0.text: HOIST CBL FOUL: the cable isn't winding correctly onto the drum, motor stops automatically. Proceed in forward flight with the load suspended (same 45/80 KIAS limits), find a suitable site, hover and slowly descend to lay the load on the ground, then recover the cable manually.

external-hoist/2/p1.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Cable and hoist malfunctions', paragraph
external-hoist/2/p1.text: HOIST OVER-TEMPERATURE: amber TEMP light on the pendant, motor current automatically limited to 80 amps — the hoist keeps working but at reduced performance. Complete the current cycle and wait for the indication to clear before resuming; prolonged operation with TEMP lit risks a hoist failure.

external-hoist/3/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Engine failure in the hover with a load on the hook', paragraph
external-hoist/3/p0.text: Where OEI hover performance capability is not required: the gross weight and hover height that would normally satisfy the Flyaway or Vertical Reject WAT charts may not actually give a safe flyaway or reject with a cable extended and a load hanging — that's a real, named caveat, not a generic warning. Recover aircraft control per the standard Vertical Reject or Flyaway procedure, then either raise the load back into the cabin, emergency-jettison it, or transition forward (same 45/80 KIAS limit), depending on conditions and load type.
external-hoist/3/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

external-hoist/1/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Key limitations', paragraph
external-hoist/1/p0.text: Minimum crew: one pilot plus one Hoist Operator. Load raising/lowering is permitted in a stationary hover or forward flight up to 45 KIAS (80 KIAS with the extended main footstep kit fitted). Maximum permissible bank angle with the cable extended is 20° — exceeding 15° of lateral pendulum angle relative to the helicopter's vertical axis can cause the overload clutch to slip, and that clutch is unlikely to function correctly if actually overloaded. Takeoff and landing with a suspended load on the hoist is prohibited.

cargo-hook/0/p0.context: System note 'Cargo Hook Operations', section 'What it is', paragraph
cargo-hook/0/p0.text: A cargo-only (Non-Human External Cargo) hook system, approved for Class B rotorcraft-load combinations — the load must be jettisonable and lifted free of land or water — Day VFR only, one pilot minimum, and only personnel actually involved in the cargo operation may be aboard. Powered from Main Bus 3; the emergency release circuit is on its own separate EMERG Bus 1, so it stays live even if the normal cargo hook power is lost.

cargo-hook/4/p0.context: System note 'Cargo Hook Operations', section 'Engine failure in the hover with a load on the hook', paragraph
cargo-hook/4/p0.text: Same caveat as with the hoist: gross weights and hover heights that satisfy the standard Flyaway or Vertical Reject WAT charts may not actually give a safe flyaway or reject with an external load hanging underneath — it's a genuinely different situation from a clean aircraft, not just a heavier one. Recover aircraft control per the standard Vertical Reject or Flyaway procedure, then jettison the load and transition forward (maximum 45 KIAS) depending on conditions.

ditching/0/p0.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'What the system is', paragraph
ditching/0/p0.text: Two forward and two aft float installations in dedicated fuselage openings, two gas distribution/inflation systems, and four immersion switches. Demonstrated and approved for ditching up to Sea State 6 (significant wave height 4–6 m) at weights up to 4800 kg — well beyond the Sea State 4 that ditching regulations actually require.
ditching/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

ditching/1/p0.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'Hard rules', paragraph
ditching/1/p0.text: The floatation system and liferafts exist for ditching only — floatation bags and liferafts must never be inflated in flight. Takeoff after ditching is prohibited. Total occupants, crew included, must not exceed 11 when forecast sea conditions along the route exceed 2.5 m significant wave height. With retractable bear paws fitted, the gear must be retracted before extended overwater flight. Bear paws, snow pads, and snow skis (Supplements 8, 45, 50) are explicitly listed as not compliant with ditching requirements — fit any of those and the ditching approval no longer applies.
ditching/1/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

ditching/2/p0.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'The ditching sequence', paragraph
ditching/2/p0.text: Preliminary: brief crew and passengers, notify ATC, transponder to 7700, seatbelt sign on, secure loose equipment, cabin doors confirmed closed (they stay closed throughout — opening them lets in the water that would otherwise be kept out), mute HTAWS, inhibit the low-height aural, life vests and harnesses on and tightened.

adelt/0/p0.context: System note 'ADELT: Crash Position Indicator with Deployable ELT', section 'What it is', paragraph
adelt/0/p0.text: A locator beacon on the left side of the tail cone, containing its own transmitter and antenna, that ejects from the aircraft in a crash — automatically, or manually at the pilot's discretion. Once deployed it transmits on two channels for two different purposes. The standard swept tone on 121.5/243.0 MHz — the classic analog distress tone — runs until battery power is exhausted, typically around 48 hours. Separately, 406.025 MHz carries an encoded digital message of the aircraft's position, sourced from the GPS/FMS via ARINC, and runs for about 24 hours.
adelt/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

ditching/2/p1.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'The ditching sequence', paragraph
ditching/2/p1.text: Approach: set the radar altimeter (height-over-water is notoriously hard to judge by eye, hence the specific caution to use RadAlt cues), wipers fast, pitot heat off, confirm FLOATS EMER armed, assess sea state and wind, establish a ditching heading and a descent profile that targets no more than 30 kt groundspeed at water contact, emergency lights on, alert everyone for impact, transmit final position, brace order over the PA, and — if power allows — establish a hover at a safe height first. Touch down cushioning the impact with the collective, aircraft level or slightly nose-up (5°), avoiding any rearward movement.

fuel-transfer-pump/0/p0.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'What it's for', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/0/p0.text: A single reversible pump, submerged in the LH tank sump, that can move fuel in either direction between the left and right main tanks through a pipeline routed via the existing intercommunication channel — no new tank wall interfaces. It self-primes in either direction within 10 seconds of power, self-stops once it can't pump any more fuel to the other side, and reports its health to the AMMC.
fuel-transfer-pump/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

fuel-transfer-pump/2/p0.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'Why unusable fuel becomes 0 kg', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/2/p0.text: Without this kit, fuel below the intercommunication channel in the tank tied to a failed engine simply can't reach the system and counts as unusable. With the Fuel Transfer Pump installed and used, that figure becomes 0 kg indicated for OEI — the pump is precisely what closes that gap. Below 160 kg is where this actually starts mattering; above that level the two tanks are already interconnected and balanced on their own.
fuel-transfer-pump/2/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

rnp-apch-lpv/0/p0.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What it is', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p0.text: Requires its own AMMS option file enabled. RNP approaches flown to LPV or LP minima (charted as RNAV(GPS) or RNAV(GNSS)) use Satellite Based Augmentation (SBAS) to fly an approach with vertical guidance down to a 200 ft decision height, with no airport-specific ground equipment required. LPV gives lateral and vertical angular guidance; LP gives lateral angular guidance paired with Baro-VNAV for the vertical path instead. The GNSS sensors feed the FMS pseudo-localizer (NLOC) and pseudo-glideslope (NGS) deviations that the AFCS actually couples to.
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

rnp-apch-lpv/0/p1.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What it is', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p1.text: Approved for day/night VFR and IFR. Maximum glide path angle 9°. Minimum airspeed to engage APP mode for these minima is 45 KIAS, and AFCS IAS mode must be engaged below 50 KIAS. Maximum ROD approaching the missed approach point is 900 fpm. Maximum airspeed at DH is 130 KIAS below 5000 ft, reducing 2 kt per 1000 ft above that — and if PWR LIM illuminates on the way down, airspeed must be reduced enough to clear it before reaching DH.
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p1.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

rnp-apch-lpv/2/p0.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'Flying it', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/2/p0.text: Before the FAF: confirm the white LPV or LP advisory, DA(H) set per the approach chart, PERFINIT executed, VNAV phase at CRUISE before the vertical path capture, and TOD correctly computed and shown. Arm NAPP (and NDCL if a deceleration profile is used) on the AFCS panel. If above the FAF altitude, the FMS captures the vertical path in Baro-VNAV down to FAF altitude, then transitions to pseudo-LOC/pseudo-GS guidance inside 2 NM of the FAF.
rnp-apch-lpv/2/p0.source_rev: RFM EP Issue 1 Rev 5; QRH EP Issue 1 Rev 3

rnp-apch-lpv/3/p1.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What a GNSS problem actually costs you', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/3/p1.text: If SBAS precision mode is lost on both GNSS sensors at once, the outcome depends on whether Baro-VNAV minima are available for that approach. If they are, FMS deviations revert automatically to LNAV/VNAV and Baro-VNAV — LPV is replaced by VGP on the PFD — and the approach can continue in coupled mode by pressing APP or DCL again, unless the aircraft is already below 1000 ft AGL, in which case discontinue regardless. If Baro-VNAV minima are not available at all, there's no fallback — discontinue the approach outright.

fuel-transfer-pump/3/p0.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'AEO limits and stopping conditions', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/3/p0.text: In AEO, transfer automatically stops the moment 1(2) FUEL LOW activates on the tank being drawn from — FUEL XFER STOPPED displays for about 10 seconds. In the two genuinely abnormal cases — a leak, or one engine burning fuel unevenly — don't use FUEL XFER unless FUEL LOW is already active on the low tank and the other tank's spare fuel is actually needed to finish the flight safely. The routine case is different: after unbalanced flight has returned to balanced, XFER can simply restore the tanks to even without any of that caution attached. On the ground, it can also be used to correct an unbalance created by single-point refueling below the intercommunication channel.

issues.evidence: When the fuel transfer is completed, a status message “FUEL XFER COMPLETE” appears on the PFD. ... The pump has the capability to self-suck in both flow directions even in case of entrapped air in the transfer hose and generate the required fuel flow within 10 seconds after power is applied.

issues.statement: FUEL XFER STOPPED displays for about 10 seconds
issues.problem: The manual does not mention a 'FUEL XFER STOPPED' message or a 10-second display duration. Instead, it states that when fuel transfer is completed, 'FUEL XFER COMPLETE' appears on the PFD.
issues.evidence: When the fuel transfer is completed, a status message "FUEL XFER COMPLETE" appears on the PFD.

rnp-apch-lpv/3/p0.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What a GNSS problem actually costs you', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/3/p0.text: A single GNSS RAIM integrity failure, or one SBAS precision-approach channel going to standby, is annunciated in the RFM as a loss of GNSS redundancy, and the instruction is to continue the approach (the GNSS sensor checks SBAS integrity every 4 seconds and may recover automatically).
